card: Tracks AddrMan's last successful connection timestamp on a per-network basis rather than globally, with a 7-day fallback to global connectivity. This prevents a node with degraded connectivity on a specific network (such as broken IPv6 or Tor) from blaming remote addresses, marking them terrible, and dropping them from address relay while other networks continue functioning. An unreachable network timeout ensures permanently disconnected networks still eventually allow address eviction.
changed_since_previous: Added a fallback mechanism (`ADDRMAN_NET_UNREACHABLE`, 7 days): if a network has seen no successful connections for 7 days or since startup, AddrMan falls back to the most recent successful connection across all networks so unreachable addresses can still be evicted.
evidence: PR description: "`m_last_good` is used to prevent recording failed attempts for addresses when it is our connectivity that is at fault. However, it is quite common that only some networks are unreachable - e.g. I have encountered it frequently that `IPv6` is unreachable, while `IPv4` works fine. In this case it is not correct to increase the failed counter for an `IPv6` address and ultimately making it `Terrible`, just because we are making `IPv4` connections."
problem: Currently, AddrMan uses a single global `m_last_good` timestamp to decide whether to record connection failures against peer addresses. If a node loses connectivity to a single network (such as IPv6 or Tor) while remaining connected via IPv4, failed attempts are counted against those addresses and eventually mark them terrible and suppress their relay, even though the connectivity fault is local to the node.

risk.why: A bug in AddrMan failure counting could alter address selection probabilities or delay evicting unreachable peers from the address manager.

summary: Tracks the timestamp of the last successful connection (`m_last_good`) per network in AddrMan rather than globally. Connection failure attempts are only recorded against an address if the node has recently established a successful connection on that address's specific network. If a network remains unreachable for more than seven days, AddrMan falls back to successful connections across any network to prevent dead addresses from occupying slots indefinitely.
